title: Desargues's Theorem: Provable from ℝ³ but Not from Plane Axioms
content:
Desargues's theorem (1639) states: if two triangles in a projective plane are in perspective from a point, then their corresponding sides meet in three collinear points. In 3D projective space, this follows from the incidence axioms alone via a lifting argument: project the triangles into two non-coplanar planes in ℝ³, where the intersection lines are forced to meet on the line of intersection of those planes. In a projective PLANE (2D), no such lift is available, and the theorem is not derivable from the projective plane axioms alone.

The Moulton plane (1902) demonstrates this independence. It takes Cartesian points ℝ² but modifies lines with positive slope: on the right half-plane (x > 0), the slope is halved. This preserves the affine plane axioms (every pair of points determines a unique line; every pair of non-parallel lines meets in a unique point) but breaks Desargues. The connection to algebra (Wedderburn 1905, Hilbert 1901): a projective plane satisfies Desargues iff it can be coordinatized by a division ring (skew field). The Moulton plane's broken coordinatization reflects the failure of the 'little Desargues' condition in the positive-slope half-plane.
mathContext: Desargues: If $O, A, B, C, A', B', C'$ are points with $O, A, A'$ collinear, $O, B, B'$ collinear, $O, C, C'$ collinear (perspectivity from $O$), then $AB \cap A'B'$, $BC \cap B'C'$, $CA \cap C'A'$ are collinear. Fails in the Moulton plane because the modification of lines with positive slope disrupts the collinearity of the three intersection points.

title: onMoultonLine: Piecewise Slope Bending at the y-Axis
content:
`onMoultonLine m b P` is defined piecewise by classical if-then-else. For m ≤ 0: P lies on the ordinary line P.2 = m·P.1 + b. For m > 0 and P.1 ≤ 0 (left half-plane): same formula. For m > 0 and P.1 > 0 (right half-plane): slope is halved, P.2 = (m/2)·P.1 + b. The boundary point (P.1 = 0) is consistent: both formulas give P.2 = b.

`MoultonCollinear P Q R` takes the disjunction: either all three points share the same x-coordinate (vertical line), or there exist m and b such that all three lie on `onMoultonLine m b`. The six helper lemmas (`onML_neg_slope`, `onML_pos_left`, `onML_pos_right`, `onML_eq_neg`, `onML_eq_pos_left`, `onML_eq_pos_right`) split the piecewise definition into constructors and destructors, avoiding repeated if-then-else case splits in the proof goals.
mathContext: Moulton line with left-slope $m$ and intercept $b$: $y = mx+b$ for $x \leq 0$, and $y = \frac{m}{2}x + b$ for $x > 0$ (when $m > 0$). Both halves pass through $(0, b)$: continuity at $x=0$. The bending factor $1/2$ is arbitrary — any $c \in (0,1)$ would work. Factor $1/2$ makes the counterexample arithmetic clean.
prerequisites: Classical.propDecidable for if-then-else on real propositions
Lean 4 def with if-then-else on Prop

title: 10 Explicit Integer Points: Exact Arithmetic and Scalar-Multiple Structure
content: The counterexample uses 10 private point definitions with integer coordinates: center O=(0,0), triangles A=(-2,3), B=(3,1), C=(0,-1) and A'=(-4,6), B'=(9,3), C'=(0,-4), and the three intersection points P=(-17,9), Q=(27,17), R=(-6,11). All are marked `private` to scope them to the MoultonPlane namespace. Integer coordinates are essential for the proof strategy: all incidence checks and the non-collinearity contradiction use `norm_num`, which does exact rational arithmetic, unlike floating-point. A key observation: A'=2A, B'=3B, C'=4C — all are scalar multiples of the originals from O=(0,0). This immediately explains why OAA', OBB', OCC' are collinear (O, X, cX are collinear for any scalar c), though the formalization still uses the full Moulton-collinearity apparatus.
mathContext: Points: $O=(0,0)$, $A=(-2,3)$, $B=(3,1)$, $C=(0,-1)$, $A'=(-4,6)=2A$, $B'=(9,3)=3B$, $C'=(0,-4)=4C$. Intersections: $P = AB \cap A'B' = (-17,9)$, $Q = BC \cap B'C' = (27,17)$, $R = CA \cap C'A' = (-6,11)$. Scalar structure means $O, A, A'$ collinear trivially ($(0,0)$, $(-2,3)$, $(-4,6)$: same direction).
prerequisites: ℝ² coordinate pair notation (Prod ℝ ℝ)

title: Perspectivity from O: Three Distinct Moulton-Collinearity Arguments
content:
The three perspectivity lemmas illustrate the three qualitatively different cases of Moulton collinearity:

`collinear_OAA'` (slope -3/2): m ≤ 0, so it's an ordinary line. All three points O=(0,0), A=(-2,3), A'=(-4,6) are on the left-half plane or the boundary. Proved by `onML_neg_slope` applied to each — one `norm_num` to verify m ≤ 0, one `ring` for the linear equation.

`collinear_OBB'` (left-slope 2/3): m > 0. O is at x=0 (left boundary, `onML_pos_left`); B=(3,1) and B'=(9,3) are at x > 0 (`onML_pos_right` with right slope 1/3). Each call requires: `norm_num` for m > 0, `norm_num` for the x-sign condition, `ring` for the equation. The right-slope equations are y = (1/3)·x + 0 = x/3: B has y=1=3/3 ✓, B' has y=3=9/3 ✓.

`collinear_OCC'` (vertical x=0): The `left` branch of MoultonCollinear. All three have P.1 = 0, closed by `simp`.
mathContext: Three perspectivity lines: $OAA'$ on $y = -\frac{3}{2}x$ (slope $-3/2$); $OBB'$ on $y = \frac{2}{3}x$ (left) / $y = \frac{1}{3}x$ (right); $OCC'$ on $x = 0$ (vertical). Each verified in one `right` + `exact` + three `onML_*` calls.

title: Intersection Points: Why Ordinary Linear Algebra Computes P, Q, R
content:
The 14 incidence lemmas verify that P, Q, R lie on the six corresponding-side Moulton lines. The key insight: all six sides (AB, A'B', BC, B'C', CA, C'A') are either negative-slope Moulton lines (coinciding with ordinary lines) or positive-slope lines whose intersection points happen to lie in the appropriate half-plane where the Moulton formula is still ordinary.

Specifically: P=(-17,9) lies on AB (slope -2/5 ≤ 0, ordinary) and A'B' (slope -3/13 ≤ 0, ordinary). R=(-6,11) lies on CA (slope -2 ≤ 0) and C'A' (slope -5/2 ≤ 0). Q=(27,17) lies on BC (left-slope 4/3 > 0, but Q is at x=27 > 0, so right-slope 2/3 applies) and B'C' (left-slope 14/9 > 0, Q at x=27 > 0, right-slope 7/9).

This is the crucial geometric insight: the bending is INVISIBLE when computing P and R (which lie on negative-slope lines), and VISIBLE only when testing whether P, Q, R themselves are collinear under a bent line.
mathContext: Side slopes: $AB$: $m=-2/5$, $A'B'$: $m=-3/13$, $CA$: $m=-2$, $C'A'$: $m=-5/2$ (all $\leq 0$, ordinary). $BC$: left-slope $4/3$, right-slope $2/3$; $B'C'$: left-slope $14/9$, right-slope $7/9$. Intersection $Q = (27, 17)$ is at $x > 0$, so both $BC$ and $B'C'$ behave with their halved slopes at $Q$.
prerequisites: Linear algebra: two-equation solve for intersection

title: desargues_fails: The Two-Case linarith Contradiction
content:
`desargues_fails` proves ¬ MoultonCollinear P Q R by contradiction via `intro h; rcases h`.

**Vertical case** (P.1 = Q.1 = R.1): P.1 = -17 ≠ 27 = Q.1, closed by `norm_num` after `simp`.

**Non-vertical case** (obtains m, b, hP, hQ, hR): Case split on m ≤ 0 vs m > 0.
- `m ≤ 0`: Both hP and hQ give ordinary line equations via `onML_eq_neg`. P at (-17,9): 9 = m(-17)+b. Q at (27,17): 17 = m(27)+b. Subtracting: 8 = 44m. Since m ≤ 0, 44m ≤ 0 < 8 — `linarith` closes it.
- `m > 0`: P.1 = -17 ≤ 0 and R.1 = -6 ≤ 0 use left formula; Q.1 = 27 > 0 uses right formula. Extract equations: 9 = m(-17)+b (from hP), 17 = (m/2)(27)+b (from hQ), 11 = m(-6)+b (from hR). Two linear_combination calls: `h1 : 11m = 2` (from hP - hR) and `h2 : 61m = 16` (from 2·hP - 2·hQ). Contradiction: 61×2 = 122 ≠ 11×16 = 176, i.e., 61×(11m) = 11×(61m) → 122 = 176. `linarith` from h1 and h2.
mathContext: Key arithmetic: $m \leq 0$ case — slope $PQ = (17-9)/(27-(-17)) = 8/44 = 2/11 > 0$, contradiction. $m > 0$ case — from $9 = -17m+b$ and $11 = -6m+b$: $-11m = 2 \Rightarrow m = 2/11$... wait: $h_1: 11m = 2$ from $(9-11) = m(-17+6) = -11m$, so $-11m = -2 \Rightarrow 11m = 2$. From $9 = -17m+b$ and $17 = 27m/2 + b$: $h_2: 61m = 16$ (multiply through). Then $61 \times (11m) = 61 \times 2 = 122$ and $11 \times (61m) = 11 \times 16 = 176$: contradiction.
prerequisites: linear_combination tactic for exact linear equality manipulation

title: moulton_counterexample: A Formal Geometry Certificate with All Incidence Data
content:
`moulton_counterexample` bundles all 22 conjuncts into a single proof term: the 3 perspectivity lemmas, the 18 incidence lemmas (P on AB and A'B', etc.), and `desargues_fails`. The proof is a single anonymous constructor `⟨collinear_OAA', collinear_OBB', ...⟩` — no tactics needed once all lemmas are established.

This pattern — a large conjunction packaging a formal counterexample — serves as a **geometry certificate**: a single Lean term whose type is a completely explicit, machine-verified statement of the failure of Desargues's theorem. Any user can check the statement by reading the type and trust that the proof verifies all arithmetic claims (slopes, intersections, non-collinearity) to arbitrary precision.

Compared to the classical pen-and-paper proof, the Lean version is longer but more reliable: every rational arithmetic step is verified by `norm_num` (which does exact rational computation), not floating-point approximation. The `linarith` contradiction is also exact: no numerical error can hide an arithmetic mistake.
mathContext: Certificate structure: $\{\text{perspectivity}\} \cup \{P, Q, R \text{ on respective side pairs}\} \cup \{\neg\text{MoultonCollinear}(P,Q,R)\}$. All 22 conditions verified exactly by norm_num + ring + linarith. No floating-point: all coordinates are rational ($\mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{R}$).
